🎭 The Agency: AI Specialists Ready to Transform Your Workflow

A complete AI agency at your fingertips - From frontend wizards to Reddit community ninjas, from whimsy injectors to reality checkers. Each agent is a specialized expert with personality, processes, and proven deliverables.

🆕 There's an app now

Agency Agents is a native app for macOS, Linux & Windows that browses the entire roster and installs it into Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Gemini, Osaurus, and more — with a click. No clone, no scripts, and it auto-updates.

→ Download the latest release · agencyagents.app

🚀 What Is This?

Born from a Reddit thread and months of iteration, The Agency is a growing collection of meticulously crafted AI agent personalities. Each agent is:

🎯 Specialized : Deep expertise in their domain (not generic prompt templates)

🧠 Personality-Driven : Unique voice, communication style, and approach

📋 Deliverable-Focused : Real code, processes, and measurable outcomes

✅ Production-Ready : Battle-tested workflows and success metrics

Think of it as : Assembling your dream team, except they're AI specialists who never sleep, never complain, and always deliver.

Option 1: Install the app (Recommended)

The fastest way in — no clone, no terminal. Agency Agents is a native desktop app (macOS · Linux · Windows) that browses the whole roster and installs agents into Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, Qwen, and Osaurus for you, then keeps them up to date.

brew install --cask msitarzewski/agency-agents/agency-agents

推荐理由 ：uv 是目前最强的 Python 包管理工具，速度快、依赖解析准确

🟢 Node.js 安装

项目依赖 Node.js，请前往官网下载安装：

版本要求 ：>= 16.0.0

📦 Python 包安装

🌐 浏览器驱动安装（可选）

如果使用默认的 CDP 模式（连接已有 Chrome 浏览器）， 无需安装浏览器驱动 。仅在使用标准 Playwright 模式时需要安装。

安装最新版 Chrome 浏览器 （版本 >= 144）， 下载地址

如果不想使用 CDP 模式，可以在 config/base_config.py 中设置 ENABLE_CDP_MODE = False 切换为标准 Playwright 模式。

📥 媒体下载（封面 / 视频 / 图文图片）

默认关闭。开启后会在爬取的同时把媒体文件下载到本地，按帖子聚合存放：

<div class="highlight highlight-source-shell notranslate position-relative overflow-auto" dir="auto" data-snippet-clipboard-copy-content="# 命令行开关

uv run main.py --platform xhs --type detail --specified_id <帖子URL或ID> --get_media true

# 或在 config/base_config.py 中设置 ENABLE_GET_MEDIA = True"> # 命令行开关

uv run main.py --platform xhs --type detail --specified_id < 帖子URL或ID > --get_media true

# 或在 config/base_config.py 中设置 ENABLE_GET_MEDIA = True

落盘结构 （ SAVE_DATA_PATH 为空时落在 data/ 下）：

<div class="snippet-clipboard-content notranslate position-relative overflow-auto" data-snippet-clipboard-copy-content="data/xhs/media/{帖子ID}/

├── cover.jpg # 封面

├── video.mp4 # 视频（B站为 DASH 合流产物）

├── 001.jpg # 图文帖的图片

└── 001_live.mp4 # 对应图片的实况随附视频（有实况时）"> data/xhs/media/{帖子ID}/

├── cover.jpg # 封面

├── video.mp4 # 视频（B站为 DASH 合流产物）

├── 001.jpg # 图文帖的图片

└── 001_live.mp4 # 对应图片的实况随附视频（有实况时）

支持平台 ：小红书、抖音、快手、B站、微博。贴吧与知乎的数据结构中没有媒体字段，暂不支持。

实况照片（Live Photo） ：抖音和小红书统一由 config/base_config.py 中的 DOWNLOAD_LIVE_PHOTO 控制，默认 True ，仅在 ENABLE_GET_MEDIA 开启时生效。设为 False 后只保存静态图，普通视频下载不受影响。实况视频与静态图使用相同的原始图片序号（如 001.jpg / 001_live.mp4 ），缺失媒体时保留序号空位。这里保存的是独立图片与随附视频，不合成手机相册的 Live Photo，也不转换为 GIF。小红书 Web 返回的实况视频可能自带水印，下载会保留该视频的原始内容。

安装 ffmpeg 后可走 DASH 路径获取最高画质（音视频分轨下载后无损合流）；未安装时自动降级为 mp4 直链，产物名为 video-durl.mp4 以便区分

清晰度由 config/bilibili_config.py 的 BILI_QN 控制（默认 80 = 1080p）；未登录或权限不足时若高清取流被拒，会自动逐档降级到实际可下载的清晰度

媒体下载失败只记录日志，不会中断爬取

已存在的文件会被跳过；需要重新下载时删掉对应目录即可

🖥️ WebUI 可视化操作界面

MediaCrawler 提供了基于 Web 的可视化操作界面，无需命令行也能轻松使用爬虫功能。

开发时需要同时启动后端 API 服务和前端 Vite 开发服务器：

uv run uvicorn api.main:app --port 8080 --reload

# 终端 2：启动前端开发服务器

npm run dev # 默认在 5173 端口启动，并代理 /api 到 8080"> # 终端 1：启动 API 服务器（默认端口 8080）

uv run uvicorn api.main:app --port 8080 --reload

# 终端 2：启动前端开发服务器

npm run dev # 默认在 5173 端口启动，并代理 /api 到 8080

启动成功后，访问 http://localhost:5173/ 即可打开 WebUI 界面。

首次打开会进行环境检测（调用 /api/env/check ），请确保后端服务已启动。如果检测失败，可点击「跳过检测」临时跳过。

In Claude Code these install as plugin commands. Where a built-in command has the same name, as /review does, use the namespaced form: /agent-skills:review .

Skills also activate automatically based on what you're doing — designing an API triggers api-and-interface-design , building UI triggers frontend-ui-engineering , and so on.

Prime Agent: A Self-Improving RLM Harness

<a id="user-content-prime-agent-a-self-improving-rlm-harness" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink:

Prime Agent: A Self-Improving RLM Harness

" href="#prime-agent-a-self-improving-rlm-harness">

Documentation •

Prime Agent is an open-source coding and research agent for general and long-running work. It is designed around two core abstractions:

The Recursive Language Model (RLM) treats context as variables ( prompt-as-a-variable ) and tools like recursive subagents as function calls ( programmatic tool /sub-agent calling ) inside a persistent REPL.

The Continual Harness stores supplemental prompts, memories, skill descriptions, and reusable subagent specifications as durable state that Prime Agent can refine through small, evidence-backed updates, local to the session by default.

Install the latest stable version with the one-command installer:

curl -fsSL https://app.primeintellect.ai/prime-agent/install.sh | sh

On Windows, install from PowerShell:

irm https: // app.primeintellect.ai / prime - agent / install.ps1 | iex

The Windows installer downloads the latest stable Windows x64 build and verifies its checksum before installation.

Why Prime Agent

Prime Agent combines a persistent Python control environment with durable harness state, so useful working context and reusable operating patterns can outlive a single chat window.

Everything is programmatic: a persistent Python REPL is the built-in model tool; file operations, shell commands, tool use, subagents, and context management happen through code.

Subagents are built in: rlm.spawn(...) spawns real child agents for parallel or background work and returns their results programmatically.

The harness can improve: /refine reviews the current trajectory and can apply small, evidence-backed updates to supplemental harness state. It never rewrites the immutable base system prompt, and recorded snapshots support rollback.

Skills can be executable: Python skills in your user configuration are imported into the kernel; repository skills provide Markdown instructions without automatic code execution.

Sessions run in the background: daemon-backed agents keep running when the terminal disconnects and can be reattached later.

Agents communicate directly: running agents can exchange messages and orchestrate one another without routing everything through the user.

Long tasks keep moving: automatic compaction, persistent goals, heartbeats, schedules, autonomous mode, and retained subagents preserve progress across turns and terminal sessions.

Connect Slack from /mcp or run /mcp login slack inside Prime Agent to search

your workspace and use Slack tools. See the Slack connector guide

for OAuth setup and troubleshooting.

Google Drive and Google Sheets

Connect Google's official Drive and Sheets MCP servers with your own Google

OAuth client: add them to mcpServers with clientId , clientSecret ,

callbackPort , and scopes , then run /mcp login <name> . See the

Google Drive and Google Sheets guide for the

Google Cloud setup and the tool mapping.

Clipboard over SSH and tmux

Prime Agent uses the local clipboard tool (such as pbcopy ) when available. In tmux it asks the attached tmux client to forward a clipboard buffer if that client advertises the Ms capability. This works with tmux's default set-clipboard external , unlike application-origin OSC 52. Without tmux, remote copies request delivery using OSC 52. Terminal requests cannot confirm that your local clipboard changed, so Prime Agent reports them as unconfirmed.

Nested tmux servers and terminals may still block delivery. An outer tmux with set-clipboard external can reject the inner server's OSC 52. In that case, run tmux set -s set-clipboard on on the outer server, or use native terminal selection (Shift-drag in most terminals; Option-drag in iTerm2) followed by Cmd-C. macOS Terminal.app does not support OSC 52; iTerm2 requires its “Applications in terminal may access clipboard” setting.

Custom certificate authorities

HTTPS requests trust your operating system's trust store together with the bundled Mozilla roots. For servers behind a custom CA, point NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS at a PEM bundle of your CA certificates — the same variable the Node/TypeScript build honors:

export NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS=/path/to/your-ca.pem

Each transport reads the variable once when its first client is initialized. The background daemon keeps the environment it started with, so run prime-agent shutdown after changing it.

Getting Started

Start Prime Agent from the repository or directory you want it to work in:

<div class="highlight highlight-source-shell notranslate position-relative overflow-auto" dir="auto" data-snippet-clipboard-copy-content="cd /path/to/project

prime-agent"> cd /path/to/project

On first launch, run /login to choose a subscription or API-key provider. Prime Agent works in the current directory and can run commands and modify files there. Use a disposable clone, clean worktree, or another checkpoint you can inspect and restore.

LifeOS is a General Purpose AI Harness for doing anything you want to do in life and work with AI. It captures who you are, what you care about, and where you're trying to go, then uses AI that knows you to help you get there.

⚠️ Your Security Is Your Responsibility

LifeOS is fundamentally one person's personal AI harness, published as-is, and it is constantly in flux: security features are added, enhanced, removed, modified and adjusted from release to release. The security of any LifeOS component, and of the system as a whole, is not guaranteed. Responsibility for the security of your system is yours, not the LifeOS authors' or contributors'.

Before anything is installed, the installer asks: "Do you understand that you are responsible for the security of your own system and that we are not responsible?" It goes ahead only if you answer yes. See SECURITY.md .

Give it to your AI. LifeOS is installed by an AI, so the install is just a prompt. Paste this into your AI coding harness — Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Hermes, or any capable agent — and it does the whole setup for you:

How is LifeOS different from using an AI harness on its own?

What harness does LifeOS run on?

Any high-end one. LifeOS is harness-agnostic by design — it's built on universal primitives (hooks, skills, context files, agentic routing), not one vendor's features. The code is TypeScript and Bash, and the core ideas — TELOS, the Algorithm, skills, memory — port to any capable agent.

Daniel builds and runs it on Claude Code , so that's the most-tested path today. But LifeOS isn't locked to it, and it's designed to run wherever your AI does.

How is this different from fabric?

Fabric is a collection of AI prompts (patterns) for specific tasks. It's focused on what to ask AI .

LifeOS is infrastructure for how your DA operates —memory, skills, routing, context, self-improvement. They're complementary. Many LifeOS users integrate Fabric patterns into their skills.

What if I break something?

Recovery is straightforward:

Back up first — Before any upgrade: cp -r ~/.claude ~/.claude-backup-$(date +%Y%m%d)

USER/ is safe — Your customizations in USER/ are never touched by the installer or upgrades

Settings merge, not overwrite — The installer only updates identity and version fields; your hooks, statusline, and custom config are preserved

Git-backed — Version control everything, roll back when needed

History is preserved — Your DA's memory survives mistakes

DA can fix it — Your DA helped build it, it can help repair it

Re-install — Run the installer again; it detects existing installations and merges intelligently

Local Model Support

Run LifeOS with local models (Ollama, llama.cpp) for privacy and cost control

Remote Access

Access your LifeOS from anywhere—mobile, web, other devices

Outbound Phone Calling

Voice capabilities for outbound calls

External Notifications

WeatherNext 2

This repo contains the code for WeatherNext 2 (WN2), the global, medium-range

atmospheric and cyclone forecasting model developed by Google DeepMind and

Google Research.

It also contains code for prior generation models

Accessing Forecast Data Feeds

If you are interested in directly accessing daily data feeds of WN2 model

outputs rather than running the model yourself, we provide them across multiple

Google Cloud

(including Earth Engine, BigQuery, and Vertex AI).

WeatherLab (including cyclone tracks).

OpenMeteo (including an API and interactive builder).

Model Guide & Documentation: Google Developers WeatherNext Guide

WeatherNext Cyclones Paper: Operational tropical cyclone forecasting

FGN/WN2 Technical Report: Skillful joint probabilistic weather

forecasting from marginals

(arXiv:2506.10772)

WeatherNext 2 Blog Post: WeatherNext 2: Our most advanced weather forecasting model

WeatherNext Cyclones Blog Post: WeatherNext: AI model achieves breakthrough in forecasting cyclones

Older Models

This repository serves as the primary home for the WeatherNext family models.

Alongside WN2, this repository also hosts the code and documentation for our

legacy and specialized models:

WeatherNext Graph : Deterministic

medium-range weather forecasting using graph neural networks. Published as

WeatherNext Gen : Diffusion-based ensemble

forecasting for medium-range weather. Published as GenCast.

Provided Pretrained Models

This repository provides code to run the different versions of WeatherNext 2 and

WeatherNext Cyclones. The only difference between them is that WN2 can also

predict 100m wind. In particular, WN2 also forecasts cyclones with the exact

same algorithm as WN Cyclones. Their weights are different due to independent

training runs.

WeatherNext 2

WeatherNext2_<2025 (Used Operationally): 0.25° resolution (~30km).

Fine-tuned on ECMWF HRES data and designed to be initialized directly from

operational HRES initial conditions rather than ERA5 reanalysis. Trained on

data through 2024. Corresponding weights files:

WeatherNext2_<2025_model{1,2,3,4}.npz .

WeatherNext Cyclones - models which reproduce the results in paper

WeatherNextCyclones_<2025 (Used Operationally): 0.25° resolution. The

model that ran live during the 2025 Atlantic hurricane season, publicly

referred to as FNV3 (NHC's postprocessed version was called GDMI). Trained

on data through 2024. The paper appendix contains a partial evaluation of

2025 in NHC basins for this model checkpoint, and how the tracker

improvement in September 2025 improved results. Corresponding weights files:

WeatherNextCyclones_<2025_model{1,2,3,4}.npz .

WeatherNextCyclones_<2024 : 0.25° resolution. Reproduces results from the

paper on 2024. Trained on data through 2023. Corresponding weights files:

WeatherNextCyclones_<2024_model{1,2,3,4}.npz .

WeatherNextCyclones_<2023 : 0.25° resolution. Reproduces results from the

paper on 2023. Trained on data through 2022. Corresponding weights files:

WeatherNextCyclones_<2023_model{1,2,3,4}.npz .

WeatherNext Cyclones Mini

WeatherNextCyclones_Mini_<2024 : 1° resolution. A lightweight version

suitable for lower memory and compute constraints (e.g., local testing or

single TPUs or GPUs). Not expected to match the performance of the larger

versions. Forecasts the same things as WeatherNext2_<2025, including

cyclones. Trained on data through 2023. Corresponding weights file:

WeatherNextCyclones_Mini_<2024.npz .

WeatherNextCyclones_Mini_<2023 : As above, but only trained on data through

2022. Corresponding weights file: WeatherNextCyclones_Mini_<2023.npz .

Evaluation results for WeatherNextCyclones_Mini can be found in the appendix

WeatherNext Cyclones Paper .

Quick Start Guide

The easiest way to get started with WeatherNext 2 is by running our interactive

Colab Notebook , which can be opened from

Colaboratory .

This notebook defaults to WeatherNext Cyclones Mini, which we recommend running

using the v5e-1 runtime, available for free as a Colab runtime. However, the

notebook can also be used to run the other models enumerated above (but these

will require a v5p accelerator).

In general, we recommend running WeatherNext 2 on TPU where possible, since its

implementation has been optimised for it. However, if choosing to run on GPU,

the attention implementation must be switched, as shown in the demo notebook.

The non-Mini models require H100 for sufficient VRAM. The Mini models should

manage inference on a P100.

Pre-trained weights and sample data are available on our Google Cloud

Inside the notebook, you will learn how to:

Automatically load the required model weights from our storage bucket.

Load initial state weather data (e.g., HRES initial conditions).

Initialize the WN2 (FGN) architecture.

Run auto-regressive rollout steps to generate a forecast prediction.

Visualize the outputs (e.g., temperature, wind speed, geopotential height).

Run the direct tracker on model outputs to obtain track data for cyclones.

Compute the training loss on model predictions and targets, and take a

gradient step.

Installation

This is research code provided as-is for the purpose of running and

experimenting with the published models. There are no guarantees of API

stability and future updates may introduce breaking changes without notice. We

recommend pinning to a specific release.

pip install git+https://github.com/google-deepmind/weathernext.git@v0.3.0

Model Weights

To run WeatherNext 2 or WeatherNext Cyclones, you will need to download the

pre-trained model weights. You can access the weights on Google Cloud

Code-Graph-RAG

Code-Graph-RAG parses a multi-language codebase with Tree-sitter, sharpened by compiler-grade frontends and runtime traces where available, builds a knowledge graph of its structure in an embedded graph database that needs no server, and lets you query, edit, and optimise that code in plain English. It works across a monorepo of mixed languages under one unified graph schema.

1. Index: cgr start --update-graph parses a repository into a knowledge graph (sped up)

2. Ask: cgr start answers questions and edits code, grounded in that graph

Latest News 🔥

Import Resolution : Enhanced resolution of imports, particularly for CommonJS renamed properties and path-qualified functions.

Incremental Builds : Ensured unchanged classes retain their field types across incremental syncs.

Python Property Access : Scoped Python property reads to their respective receivers.

Cross-Language Imports : Rejected cross-language internal import targets to improve clarity.

Constructor Initialisation : Correctly handled attribute field initializers in TS/JS, Java and C# constructors.

See NEWS.md for the full history.

What It Does

Point Code-Graph-RAG at a repository and it reads every source file, extracts functions, classes, methods, modules, and the relationships between them, and stores the result as an interconnected graph. Once the graph exists you can:

Ask questions about the codebase in natural language and get answers grounded in the real structure.

Retrieve the actual source of any function, class, or method by name or by intent.

Edit code through the agent with AST-based surgical patching and a diff preview before anything changes.

Optimise code against language best practices or your own coding standards.

Find dead code by walking call and reference edges from entry points.

Search and rewrite structurally by AST pattern with ast-grep.

Overlay runtime behaviour: trace a test run (or pull production eBPF profiles) with cgr trace and merge the calls that actually happened into the graph, exposing dispatch that static analysis cannot see.

How It Works

The system has two components:

Multi-language parser. A Tree-sitter based parser reads the codebase and ingests functions, classes, methods, modules, and their relationships into the graph under a single language-agnostic schema. Where a toolchain is available, compiler-grade frontends layer exact facts on top (libclang for C/C++, go/types for Go, and opt-in Roslyn, javac and Jedi for C#, Java and Python), and dynamic tracing merges calls observed at runtime. Tree-sitter stays the backbone: a trace only sees code that ran, and a compiler frontend only covers what its toolchain can build.

RAG system ( codebase_rag/ ). An interactive CLI that turns natural language into Cypher queries, retrieves matching code, and drives AI-powered editing and optimisation.

<div class="snippet-clipboard-content notranslate position-relative overflow-auto" data-snippet-clipboard-copy-content="Source Code -> Tree-sitter Parser -> AST Analysis -> Knowledge Graph

User Query -> AI Model (Cypher Gen) -> Cypher Query -> Graph Results -> Response"> Source Code -> Tree-sitter Parser -> AST Analysis -> Knowledge Graph

User Query -> AI Model (Cypher Gen) -> Cypher Query -> Graph Results -> Response

The graph is stored in an embedded SQLite file by default. Memgraph and Neo4j are opt-in backends that run the same Cypher; Graph Backends compares them.

See the Architecture Overview and Graph Schema for the full picture.

Supported Languages

Python, TypeScript, TSX, JavaScript, Rust, Go, Java, C, C++, C#, PHP, Lua, Dart, and Julia are fully supported. Scala is in development, and Ruby, Kotlin, Swift, Elixir, Haskell, Solidity, Bash, and Nix have structural support (modules, functions, classes where the language has them, and imports) through the pluggable ast-grep tier. See the Language Support matrix for per-language capabilities.

items.title: Are today's PG-13 films more violent than 1980s R-rated films?
items.summary: Are today's PG-13 films more violent than 1980s R-rated films?（来源：Hacker News）
items.content:
Are today's PG-13 films more violent than 1980s R-rated films?

I measured the gunfire in 1,196 box office hits and how violent audiences judge 5,680 films to be, from the 1980s to today

Stephen Follows

Nov 16, 2026

A 2013 study in the journal Pediatrics concluded that gun violence in PG-13 films had more than tripled since 1985, and that recent PG-13 movies actually had more gun violence than R-rated ones.

This caused quite a stir at the time and seemed to confirm everything some parents worried about when it comes to cinema and violence. However, after researching the topic, I don’t think what people took away from it reflects what's really happening on-screen.

Today’s PG-13 films are not more violent than the R-rated films of the 1980s. They contain a little less gunfire (about four-fifths as much), and they are nowhere near as violent.

It’s a bit of a long article, so let’s start with a pretty gif as a TL;DR.

Each dot is a film, placed by how much audible gunfire it has (left to right) and how violent viewers judge it to be (bottom to top). The background colours show which rating’s films are most concentrated in each part of the map, and the large dots follow each rating’s middle film, with the US on the left and the UK on the right.

Look at the orange dots (i.e. PG-13 in America and 12A in Britain). They move a long way to the right, into the same range of gunfire as the adult ratings, but stay well below them on violence.

Ok, let’s get into the details of the data.

Gathering signals

The original study counted gun violence by asking people to watch half of the 30 top-grossing films of each year and mark every five-minute stretch in which a gun was used violently.

That method certainly counts when a trigger is pulled, but not what happens next. I don't think that fully matches up with what people mean when they call a film “violent”.

So I built my own measures.

Gunfire . I used a detector that listens to each film’s soundtrack for gunshots and looks at its pictures for guns being fired, which I ran across the 30 highest-grossing US films each year from 1985 to 2025 (1,196 films total). It was trained to match human coders who had counted gun violence by hand in 448 of those films.

Violence . This looks at how violent a film feels on a scale of 0 to 100. A film's score is its place among all the films in my data, so a score of 80 means it is more violent than 80% of the 5,274 films that have a score.

Is there as much shooting?

The chart below shows gun-violence scenes per hour in the 30 top-grossing US films of each year, by rating.

In the late 1980s, PG-13 movies had an average of one gun-violence scene every two hours. That works out as 0.48 gun-violence scenes per hour. By the middle of the 2010s, that had risen to 1.70 per hour and was on a par with R-rated movies.

It has eased back a little since, to 1.34 per hour in 2020-25, against 1.85 for the R-rated hits of 1985-89.

Taking 2015-25 against 1985-94 as a whole, PG-13 films have 78% of the old R-rated level.

Is it as brutal?

This alone isn’t enough, as we have to be precise about what we’re actually measuring. My gunfire is tracking the act of a gun being fired and cannot take account of what happens to the bullet, or what/whom it hits. And what the audience sees after the shot is what most parents mean when they call a film “violent”.

The chart below shows my measure of violence for top-grossing PG-13 films in each period, with the R-rated hits of 1985-94 on the right for comparison.

The orange band is where the two meet. Between 2015 and 2025, 28% of PG-13 hits score between 60 and 79, against 36% of the 1985-94 R films. The difference is all in the red. 30% of those R films score 80 or more, and not one of today’s PG-13 hits does.

The same pattern holds well beyond the box office hits. Here are the average scores for all 4,523 films.

For forty years, the average PG-13 film has scored between 36 and 47, and the average R film between 58 and 71. PG-13 rose a little in the 2000s and has since fallen back, and the two lines have never crossed or come close. The original study found more gun violence in PG-13 films, and so do I. What I don’t find is PG-13 films becoming as violent as R.

Shooting without the blood

Putting the two measures together shows how far apart they’ve drifted. Each dot below is a period of top-grossing films, placed by how much gunfire they have (left to right) and how often they score 80 or more for violence (bottom to top), with each rating’s periods joined in time order.

The PG-13 path runs along the floor to the right without moving up. Today’s PG-13 films sit below the 1980s R films, firing nearly as many shots and almost never scoring 80 or more.

To see what that looks like on screen, I compared R-rated films with their PG-13 remakes or sequels, which share a story and an audience. The pairs are RoboCop (1987) and RoboCop (2014), Total Recall (1990) and Total Recall (2012), Die Hard (1988) and Live Free or Die Hard (2007), and Terminator 2: Judgment Day (1991) and Terminator Genisys (2015).

The shooting is in the same range.

RoboCop has 7.2 gun-violence scenes per hour in 1987 and 5.0 in 2014.

Die Hard has 5.2 and its PG-13 sequel 4.0.

Terminator Genisys (5.0) almost matches Terminator 2 (5.2).

I took 20 bursts of gunfire from each film and looked at what we see on screen in the three seconds after the shooting started. In the R-rated originals, a person was visibly hit in 15% of gunfire moments, and in 58% of those we saw blood. In the PG-13 films, 5% of moments showed a person being hit, and all were bloodless.

Die Hard is the exception - its PG-13 sequel shows slightly more people being hit than the original does, though without blood.

The other difference is what’s being shot at.

In the PG-13 films, 21% of gunfire moments are aimed at robots or synthetic soldiers, against 2% in the originals, and in the 2012 Total Recall it’s 60%.

Home / News / Hyperscale data centers’ energy consumption, carbon emissions newly estimated by researchers

Environment & Climate Health

Hyperscale data centers’ energy consumption, carbon emissions newly estimated by researchers

Maya Brownstein

November 16, 2026

Hide caption

Show caption

class="with-caption__caption"

id="captionFeaturedImage2"

Aerial view of a data center campus in Hutto, Texas. BackyardProduction / iStock

Jump to Section

New research reveals the electricity consumption and carbon emissions behind America’s hyperscale data centers rivals that of some U.S. states

For immediate release: November 16, 2026

Boston, MA—Over the course of a year, hyperscale data centers (HDCs)—the largest and most powerful class of data centers, supporting services such as cloud computing, large language model training, and global deployment of artificial intelligence (AI) tools—are powered mostly by fossil fuels and use as much electricity as entire U.S. states, according to a new study led by Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health and the Harvard Data Science Initiative . The study provides one of the first facility-level estimates of HDCs’ electricity use and carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions since the rise of AI.

The study was published Nov. 16 in Nature Sustainability.

“Data centers are growing incredibly fast, driven largely by AI, and decisions about where to build them and how to power them are being made right now. But there’s very little facility-level information about their environmental footprint,” said lead author Gianluca Guidi , postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Biostatistics . “Our study helps fill that gap.”

“Our goal is to give the public, policymakers, investors, and developers a much more concrete, up-to-date picture than was available before,” added corresponding author Francesca Dominici , Clarence James Gamble Professor of Biostatistics, Population, and Data Science and director of the Harvard Data Science Initiative. “Decisions about where data centers go and how they’re powered are critical environmental and public health decisions, and they should be made with good data.”

While data centers are known to require significant electricity to run, few studies have examined this topic facility by facility, estimating not just how much electricity each HDC uses, but what fuels generated this electricity. For this study, the researchers used satellite imagery to build a list of 403 HDCs across the U.S. and estimated annual electricity consumption for each facility between May 2024 and April 2025 under a range of operating scenarios. They then used Environmental Protection Agency data to attribute carbon emissions to each HDC based on the mix of power plants in its regional grid.

The study found that these HDCs, depending on how hard they were running, together used between 68 and 99 terawatt-hours of electricity—with the upper estimate approaching the amount some states, such as Indiana, Michigan, and Tennessee, use in a year. During the study period, HDC electricity demand corresponded to approximately 1.8% of total U.S. electricity consumption, and was associated with about 25.7 million metric tons of CO2—an amount two to three times higher than an earlier estimate for 2018.

Today, electricity demand and carbon emissions are likely much higher than they were during the study period, the researchers say.

“What we’re seeing is already striking, but it’s only a snapshot of a rapidly expanding industry,” Guidi said. “The data center boom hasn’t slowed down since our study period ended in April 2025. New facilities have been built, existing campuses have expanded, and demand for AI computing continues to grow. That means the electricity use and carbon footprint we’re reporting could already be substantially larger now in 2026.”

The study also found that roughly 54% of the electricity powering the HDCs was generated by fossil fuels—mainly natural gas (38%) and coal (15%)—and about a quarter of the electricity was in grid regions dirtier than average. The researchers noted substantial regional differences, with some HDCs relying much more heavily on carbon-intensive electricity than others. Many of the facilities were concentrated in geographic areas where electricity is generated heavily by coal-fired power plants.

The researchers also noted that just four states—Virginia, Oregon, Ohio, and Iowa—accounted for more than half of the electricity use studied.

The study had limitations, including that there wasn’t enough available data to study all HDCs in the U.S., and that the data did not allow them to differentiate between power used for general-purpose versus AI-specialized operations at each HDC.

The researchers also noted that the study didn’t directly measure the health effects associated with HDCs, but that is a subject they plan to pursue in future research.

“Quantifying health impacts is an important next step,” said Dominici. “First, carbon dioxide drives climate change, which affects health through heat waves, wildfire smoke, flooding, and other pathways. Second, the fossil fuel power plants in the regional electricity systems associated with this demand also release other pollutants, such as fine particulate matter, nitrogen oxides, and sulfur dioxide, that are directly linked to heart and lung disease and premature death. So when data centers draw heavily on fossil fuel power, the people living near and downwind of those power plants may bear health costs, even if they’re far from the data center itself.”

Article information

“Assessing the Carbon Emissions and Energy Consumption of US Hyperscale Data Centers,” Gianluca Guidi, Francesca Dominici, Tiziano Squartini, Callaway Sprinkle, Jonathan Gilmour, Kevin Butler, Eric Bell, Scott Delaney, Falco J. Bargagli-Stoffi, Nature Sustainability, November 16, 2026, doi: 10.1038/s41893-026-01985-7

items.title: Hugging Face and OpenRouter join forces to make open-weight models easy to run
items.summary: Hugging Face and OpenRouter join forces to make open-weight models easy to run（来源：Hacker News）
items.content:
Back to Articles

Hugging Face and OpenRouter join forces to make open-weight models easy to run

November 16, 2026

Update on GitHub

Célina Hanouti celinah Follow

Victor Mustar victor Follow

Bertrand Chevrier kramp Follow

Lucain Pouget Wauplin Follow

Pierric Cistac pierric Follow

Eliott Coyac coyotte508 Follow

Julien Chaumond julien-c Follow

:last-child]:mb-0">

Hugging Face and OpenRouter are teaming up to make open-weight models easy to run. Every major open-weight release is already being published on the Hugging Face Hub, and OpenRouter serves those models at scale, routing each request across 80+ providers based on live measurements of each one. Together, every open-weight model on the Hub that a provider serves can be called with your Hugging Face token, through the same API, with the best provider picked for each request.

Today, we are switching Inference Providers from our own custom router to OpenRouter's. Requests made to language models now go through OpenRouter, which picks the best provider for each call based on live price, speed and reliability, and retries on another provider if the first one fails. Your code stays the same.

Run them with the tools you already use

The router supports OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs and Anthropic's Messages API for every chat model, whatever the provider behind it. Pick your coding agent or SDK and a model, then copy the steps, or copy the whole setup as a prompt for your agent:

Setup guides for Claude Code , Codex , OpenCode , Pi and Hermes Agent

The same Hugging Face token also gives you storage with Storage Buckets , compute with Jobs and dedicated inference with Inference Endpoints . PRO, Team and Enterprise plans include monthly credits for compute and inference.

How open-weight models are used

On OpenRouter, open-weight models went from 26.8% of the tokens served in October 2025 to 71.7% at the end of September 2026, after peaking at 77.5% in July ( OpenRouter, October 2026 ). Over the same period, weekly open-weight volume grew more than 60-fold, against almost tenfold for closed models. This week, the most used model on OpenRouter is an open-weight one, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, with 59.2 trillion tokens ( rankings ).

Open-weight models cost about four times less on average: $0.28 per million input tokens and $1.62 per million output tokens, against $1.27 and $6.36 for closed models.

The best open-weight models still trail the best proprietary ones on the hardest benchmarks. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index , Kimi K3.1 Pro, the best open-weight model, scores 46 against 65 for Claude Fable 5.2, at about a seventh of the cost per task ($3.68 against $26.54). For a lot of workloads, that trade-off is worth it.

Routing powered by OpenRouter

OpenRouter serves more than 800 trillion tokens a month to over 10 million users, across 600+ models from 80+ providers. Its routing is based on live measurements of every provider across that traffic.

OpenRouter recently rebuilt its provider routing : instead of only looking at the lowest list price, it sends each request to the provider with the best mix of price, speed and reliability.

When a provider slows down or starts failing, traffic moves away from it until it recovers, and a failed try is retried on the next best provider inside the same call. In OpenRouter's measurements, the new routing cut capacity errors by 46% and improved time to first token by 16.9% and throughput by 16.3%.

Before, Inference Providers picked one provider for your request and returned its error if it failed. Now, the request is retried on another provider. You can still choose a policy or a provider with a suffix on the model id:

zai-org/GLM-5.3 # default: best mix of price, speed and reliability

zai-org/GLM-5.3:fastest # highest throughput

zai-org/GLM-5.3:cheapest # lowest price

zai-org/GLM-5.3:novita # only Novita

Routing is also cache-aware: a conversation stays on the provider that holds its prompt cache. To make it explicit, send a stable UUID per conversation in the X-HF-Session-Id header (see the prompt caching guide ).

Pricing doesn't change: you pay the provider's price on your Hugging Face bill, and Hugging Face doesn't add a markup on top of it. PRO users get $2 of credits every month, and Team and Enterprise organizations get $2 per seat. See Pricing and Billing for the details.

Image, video and audio generation

Image, video, and audio generation continue to work exactly as before, directly through Hugging Face Inference Providers without going through OpenRouter. You can keep using the same token and API, and access tens of thousands of LoRAs .

See where your requests go

On model pages, you can chat with the model right away in the widget. Two new tabs show what's behind it: Providers lists every provider OpenRouter can route the model to, with its input and output price, speed and uptime over the last 24 hours, and Metrics shows the best price, throughput, time to first token, context length and uptime among them:

Your usage overview breaks your spend down by the provider each request went to:

In your settings , you can turn off any provider you don't want: the router never sends your requests there. Organizations have the same settings, and they apply to every request billed to the organization.

Breaking change: custom provider keys

Requests to language models now go through OpenRouter and are billed to your Hugging Face account or organization, so you can no longer use your own API key for a provider with these models. You can still pick a provider with a suffix on the model id ( model:provider ) or turn providers off in your settings, and your code stays the same. Custom keys for image and video providers keep working.

This is the first step of our partnership with OpenRouter. Next:

Connect your OpenRouter account to Hugging Face.

More tasks routed through OpenRouter.

Try a model , or read the Inference Providers docs to get started.

items.summary: Corporations Are Using Refunds of Trump's Tariffs on Executive Bonuses（来源：Hacker News）
items.content:

President Donald Trump announces tariffs at the White House in April 2025.

Corporations Are Using Trump’s Tariff Refunds on Bonuses Rather Than Reimbursing Consumers

Stanley Black & Decker is getting at least $298 million in tariff refunds. The parent firm of TJ Maxx received $331 million. Both companies, and others, are using the money for corporate bonuses instead of repaying shoppers.

src="https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/01/20171213_portraits00280-robert-faturechi-sized.jpg?w=50"

class="wp-block-propublica-byline__photo"

src="https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/Nick-McMillan-1x1-1.jpg?w=50"

class="wp-block-propublica-byline__photo"

by Robert Faturechi and Nick McMillan

November 16, 2026, 6:00 am

Change Appearance Auto Light Dark

When Stanley Black & Decker, one of the world’s largest tool companies, got hit with President Donald Trump’s tariffs last year, the firm made clear that it would be sharing the pain with its customers.

The Connecticut-based company raised prices again and again, moves its executives said were necessary because of the new fees on imports.

Now, after the Supreme Court struck down Trump’s most sweeping tariffs earlier this year, the company is getting at least $298 million refunded. Instead of sharing that bounty with its customers, however, the firm has chosen different recipients:

Its own leaders.

The company is one of at least nine that have disclosed that they are using their refunds not to pay back the cash-strapped consumers who generally covered much of the tariff costs through higher prices, but to give bonuses, according to a ProPublica analysis of thousands of securities filings and earnings calls for publicly traded companies.

Other recognizable companies include the owners of discount department stores TJ Maxx and Marshalls and the golf equipment brand Titleist.

Dozens of other firms have said little about how they plan to use the money other than to characterize the windfall as the kind of earnings they use to determine executive bonuses.

The Trump administration has not publicly detailed which companies are getting the roughly $170 billion in refunds or how much they’ve asked for, and it has denied ProPublica’s requests for this information. But reporters found some of these details while reviewing the disclosures of thousands of publicly traded companies.

Some have described vague plans to pay the money forward by, for example, “returning tariff refunds to our members through pricing,” though they generally don’t say whether that involves price cuts or limiting future increases. Others are paying back businesses they sold products to because they had itemized receipts that detailed the tariff markups.

But consumers hoping for refunds appear to be largely out of luck. With the help of artificial intelligence, ProPublica identified companies that said they planned to refund customers with their tariff windfalls. Almost all of them deal with other businesses, not consumers.

“Executive bonuses are probably the least just way to use this money because it wasn’t anything the executives did that they should be rewarded for. It was a government mistake that resulted in a refund,” said Gregory Germain, a corporate law professor at Syracuse University. “It really explains why it’s so important for the government, when they’re doing something like this, to think it through to make sure consumers don’t pay extra money and not get it back.”

The chain reaction that led to these bonuses began in the first months of Trump’s second term. In February 2025, Trump declared a national emergency over illegal drugs coming in across the border and unilaterally announced new tariffs on goods from the countries he deemed responsible: Canada, Mexico and China.

Then, in April, he declared a second national emergency, this one over the U.S. trade deficit — the fact that the U.S. was importing more than it exported. Declaring it “Liberation Day,” Trump unveiled a poster in the Rose Garden detailing his most sweeping tariffs yet on goods from more than 100 countries.

“Executive bonuses are probably the least just way to use this money.”

Gregory Germain, corporate law professor at Syracuse University

Those tariffs remained in place, with some tweaks, until earlier this year when the Supreme Court struck them down, ruling that Trump had needed congressional approval to impose them.

That left the federal government scrambling to figure out how to refund billions in duties it had collected over the prior year on more than 53 million imported shipments. U.S. Customs and Border Protection set up an online application system. But only the direct payers of the tariffs — called the “importers of record” — are eligible to apply, not the businesses and consumers who took a hit downstream.

The New York Federal Reserve Bank, which analyzed the prices of a broad swath of goods, found that 26% of the tariff costs were eaten by American customers; a study from Harvard Business School put the estimate at 43%. One study estimated that Trump’s tariffs cost typical American households about $1,000 last year.

I searched the open and closed issues for a related report.

I removed credentials, tokens, private paths, and sensitive target data.

Evidence, artifacts, or reconstruction

Observed behavior

A HAR recorded by Playwright 1.64.1 becomes unreadable when a request fails. REA rejects the entire capture with HAR schema validation failed: minimum (must be >= 0) , including its successful requests.

Reproduction

Executed against main 3676ec632 on Windows x64, Node 24.22.1, Playwright 1.64.1, Chrome 157.0.8103.52:

Start a local HTTP fixture server. Serve a normal HTML page. For /broken , close the request socket before writing response headers. For /partial , send status 200 with Content-Length: 10000 , write incomplete , then close the socket.

Record a full HAR using a fresh Playwright browser context. Navigate to the page, then fetch both endpoints, catching the fetch/body errors. Close the context to finish the HAR.

Decode the HAR using REA's decodeHarCapture(text, []) .

The baseline refuses /log/entries/1/timings/send . A first implementation that admitted only status -1 still refused the partial response at /log/entries/2/timings/receive .

Before headers

net::ERR_EMPTY_RESPONSE

send/wait/receive = -1

Incomplete body

net::ERR_CONTENT_LENGTH_MISMATCH

receive = -1; send/wait are nonnegative

Expected behavior

Impact and scope

Both locally reproduced failure modes prevent inspection of otherwise useful captures. This report covers Playwright 1.64.1 on Chromium. Other exporters, browser engines and versions are unverified. #10336 concerns bracketed IPv6 addresses and does not cover these timing fields.

ChatGPT for Academic Researchers ChatGPT for Academic Researchers ChatGPT for Academic Researchers

November 16, 2026 · Research · Science

Broadening access to AI for scientists

We’re expanding the ChatGPT for Academic Researchers program to give up to 200,000 researchers worldwide free access to ChatGPT.

The program began as a pilot in July. Applications for the next round open Monday, November 23. We’ll award 50,000 new grants to eligible researchers on a first-come, first-served basis. Each grant gives the recipient and up to two collaborators free access to ChatGPT Plus. If you’re already on the waitlist and qualify, we’ll email you before applications open with instructions for activating your account.

Participants can use OpenAI’s frontier models and get training on how to use ChatGPT in their research. By default, we don’t use data shared through the program to train our models.

Waitlist signups by country or territory as of November 12, 2026. Darker colors indicate more signups on a logarithmic scale.

What we learned from the pilot

20,000 researchers in 33 countries have joined the program since the pilot began in July. Shuqi Li, a researcher at Brigham and Women’s Hospital and Harvard Medical School, looks for new drug targets that could ultimately shorten tuberculosis treatment. He is exploring whether ChatGPT can help link lab and patient data to speed up antibiotic development. Arthur Porto, assistant curator of AI biodiversity at the Florida Museum of Natural History, and his team uses AI tools to turn photographs of museum specimens into searchable databases. They also created a 3D model of a butterfly whose wings change color as you turn it, just like the real specimen.

We’re also publishing Science at the Frontier: How Scientists Use ChatGPT , new research from our Economic Research team examining how more than 1,800 researchers used ChatGPT during the program’s summer pilot. Surveyed participants estimated that, without AI, the same research work at the same quality would have taken nearly twice as long.

We want more researchers to have the tools and support to pursue ambitious questions and make discoveries that improve people’s lives. That is central to our mission of ensuring that AGI benefits all of humanity.

Building on what we learned

The program’s summer pilot helped us understand how researchers use ChatGPT and how we can improve their experience. Based on feedback from researchers, we’re moving away from lottery-based selection. For the next round, we’ll provide access to the first 50,000 applications who meet the eligibility requirements.

The pilot gave researchers access to ChatGPT Pro. When we reviewed pilot usage, we found that most participants would have stayed within ChatGPT Plus usage limits. Based on that finding, we’re offering Plus for new grants so we can extend access to more research teams.

Each grant for this round covers the recipient and up to two collaborators, supporting up to 150,000 researchers. Our goal for the program as a whole is to reach 200,000 researchers, double the goal we announced when the pilot launched in July.

We’ll continue learning from participants about the application process, the capabilities they need, and the support that helps them use these tools in their research. This feedback will help us refine the program and shape future rounds.

Supporting researchers across fields

Different scientific fields will use AI in different ways, and researchers will need different kinds and levels of support. We’re working with scientific communities to understand those needs and shape our tools, training, and programs around them.

Our support also includes helping scientific communities turn AI-generated results into deeper understanding and new discoveries. In mathematics, we contributed $5 million to a new Simons Foundation initiative ⁠ to help mathematicians examine, understand, and build on results produced by AI.

We’re also providing different ways for researchers and institutions to access our tools. ChatGPT for Academic Researchers is just one way we’re helping researchers access advanced AI tools.

Through ChatGPT Edu ⁠ (opens in a new window) , universities can give their campus communities access to ChatGPT for research, teaching, and learning, with tools for analyzing data and administrative controls for managing access.

For researchers working in biology, GPT‑Rosalind ⁠ brings together specialized biological reasoning and access to scientific tools and databases. items.title: The Many Meanings of "Stack"
items.summary: The Many Meanings of "Stack"（来源：Hacker News）
items.content:
Author’s note: Hacker News comments here .

With regards to “same word different meaning”, the term stack comes up top (pun intended). This post is not written to be comprehensive, but I hope it provides sufficient detail to save you the few hours I spent being very confused.

Stack vs queue

The stack is a data structure where it’s easy to remove the item most recently-added to the collection (Last-In-First-Out or LIFO). Think of a stack of pancakes, where it’s easy to remove the pancake at the top. This is in contrast to the queue , where it’s easy to remove the item that’s been in the collection for the longest time (First-In-First-Out or FIFO).

From Crafting Interpreters A nice contrast arises when the data structures are used to traverse a graph. If you use a stack you’ll go depth-first (DFS), with a queue breadth-first (BFS).

Stack vs heap

To enable code execution, the OS allocates a region in memory for the running process. The stack is for local variables, function arguments and return addresses - the size of these objects are known at compile time. This is in contrast with the heap , which is used for dynamically-located data such as lists and dictionaries.

From OS: Three Easy Pieces With regards to performance, it’s faster to use the stack since there’s very little overhead - the stack is managed by simply changing a counter (the stack pointer). Allocating on the heap takes a bit more work. We’ll need to find a free contiguous memory block of the right size, update the list of free blocks, and free the block when no longer needed.

For further details, Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces discusses memory allocation of a process in Section 4.3. Computer Systems: A Programmer’s Perspective goes through dynamic memory allocation in Section 9.9. For a more intuitive (or perhaps, less counter-intuitive) way of thinking about stack growth on the x86, Eli Bendersky has a helpful post .

Stack-based VM

The term virtual machine is also overloaded. For our purposes, we’re referring to the process virtual machine which lets you run the same instructions across different OS or different processors. For example, you can run Java bytecode on any platform that supports the JVM, and WebAssembly on any web browser. This is in contrast to the system virtual machine , which lets you play Windows games on a Linux machine ( example from Bob Nystrom ).

A stack-based VM executes instructions by using a stack in the sense of “stack vs queue” above, through push (add to stack) and pop (remove from stack) operations. In fact, both the JVM and WebAssembly use stack-based VMs. This is in contrast with a register-based VM , which uses virtual registers and maps more naturally to physical registers.

The second part of Crafting Interpreters involves implementing a stack-based VM. Lua moved from a stack-based to a register-based VM in the upgrade from 4.0 to 5.0. The paper describes a number of language optimizations in the upgrade, but the VM change alone shows significant performance gains. Linus Lee has a thoughtful post on Lua internals based on the paper.

Stack-based calling convention

A calling convention defines how function calls in a programming language operate at the machine-code level. With a stack-based calling convention , function arguments and return values are passed on the stack in the sense of “stack vs heap” above. This is in contrast to a register-based calling convention , which uses physical registers and allows state be kept in registers across function calls.

Go moved from a stack-based to a register-based calling convention in the upgrade from 1.16 to 1.17. The stack-based calling convention has the benefit of being simple - all platforms use the same conventions and thus no processor-specific register details are needed. The register-based calling convention, however, benefits from higher throughput as accessing arguments in registers is faster than on the stack.

Details on the upgrade can be found in the proposal , with an approachable post on the topic by Menno Finlay-Smits (with assembly and benchmarks!). What’s also worth a read is the switch to a multiple ABI mechanism done in parallel to support the change.

Skin-attached bioadhesive patch enabling ultrasound deep brain stimulation and real-time electrophysiological monitoring for REM sleep enhancement

Wearable bioelectronic interfaces capable of simultaneous neural sensing and targeted deep brain modulation remain limited by the lack of non-invasive technologies with sufficient spatial precision and mechanical stability for continuous operation. Here we report NEUSLeeP, a flexible skin-attached bioadhesive patch integrating electrophysiological sensing with transcranial focused ultrasound neuromodulation. The system incorporates a tunable concentric-ring ultrasound array, conformal hydrogel electrophysiological electrodes, and compliant interconnects within a soft substrate optimized for stable overnight operation. This integrated architecture enables spatially selective modulation and concurrent electrophysiological monitoring of deep brain structures, specifically the subthalamic nucleus during natural sleep. In a 28-participant study, NEUSLeeP demonstrated robust monitoring of sleep performance with precise-targeted neuromodulation of STN resulting in an increase in REM duration by 4.6% and reducing REM latency by 24%. This work establishes an ultrasound bioelectronic platform for non-invasive, spatiotemporally precise modulation and monitoring of deep neural circuits for neuroscience and bioelectronic medicine. items.summary: Intel Diamond Rapids Xeon Gets Up to 1.6TB/S of RAM Bandwidth, 1.28GB of Cache（来源：Hacker News）
items.content:
Intel Diamond Rapids Xeon Gets Up to 1.6TB/s of Memory Bandwidth and 1.28GB of Cache Across 256 P-Cores

by Harold Fritts

on November 16, 2026

Enterprise ◇

Intel laid out its high-performance computing plans for SC26, with Diamond Rapids, its next-generation Xeon server architecture, at the center. Intel says the platform will scale to 256 performance cores with up to 1.6TB/s of memory bandwidth and up to 1.28GB of last-level cache. The outline came from Jeff McVeigh, vice president and general manager of Data Center Strategic Programs, and it also covers the Intel GPU D-series, HPC software, silicon photonics, and quantum development. Intel gave no launch date for Diamond Rapids.

Diamond Rapids CPU Architecture

Intel describes Diamond Rapids , which it detailed at Hot Chips as an 18A-P design, as pairing higher compute density with more memory bandwidth, larger caches, and expanded CPU acceleration. Intel Advanced Performance Extensions (APX) are aimed at per-thread performance, and what Intel calls a unified memory fabric delivers the 1.6TB/s figure. Intel has not said how many memory channels or what memory speed sit behind that number, or whether it applies per socket.

The architecture also supports Intel AVX 10.2 and enhanced Intel Advanced Matrix Extensions (Intel AMX). Intel calls the next-generation Xeon the only x86 server CPU with built-in matrix compute for HPC and AI workloads. For reference on core count, the top AMD EPYC Venice parts we reviewed carry 256 Zen 6c cores per socket.

McVeigh framed the roadmap around mixed systems in which CPUs orchestrate workflows and run parallel communication libraries while accelerators take the AI work, writing that the future of HPC is “open, heterogeneous and balanced.”

Intel GPU D-series and HPC Software

The Intel GPU D-series pairs AI acceleration with double-precision (FP64) compute in an air-cooled PCIe card, with datatype support running from FP4 and MXFP4 through FP64. The Intel-branded GPU D270 carries 160GB of LPDDR5X with 1.5TB/s of memory bandwidth, and partner-designed configurations scale to 480GB. Intel’s argument for research sites centers on memory capacity, since keeping larger working datasets on the card reduces the partitioning and host-to-accelerator transfers that slow scientific workflows, and Intel also pitches the card for always-on AI agents that generate code and launch compute jobs.

Intel is running two live demos of the GPU D270, the D-series card formerly code-named Crescent Island, at its SC26 booth. The first is a seismic imaging mini-application from Veridien that was ported from HIP and CUDA to SYCL in less than a month, and Intel says 90% of its kernels ran well with no Intel-specific optimization. The second splits an inference pipeline between D270 cards that handle prefill and SambaNova SN50 units that handle decode, with Xeon 6 and Xeon 6+ processors orchestrating.

Intel also published comparisons against NVIDIA’s RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition. On FP64 financial workloads, it claims up to 5.9x the throughput on European Monte Carlo, 5.6x on European Black-Scholes, 4.6x on binomial pricing, and 1.92x on American Black-Scholes, with the D270 at 350W and the NVIDIA card at 600W. For inference, Intel claims up to 29% lower latency on Drex v2.0 and 1.12x the output token throughput on Qwen3-30B-A3B at FP8.

These are vendor results on pre-production silicon, and we did not run or audit them. Intel’s financial test configuration lists eight NVIDIA cards against a single D270 and does not say whether the results are normalized per card, and the NVIDIA inference runs used an AWS virtual machine.

On software, Intel says it will keep investing in Intel MPI, Fortran, compiler optimizations, and oneAPI so existing parallel codebases keep running well on mixed CPU and GPU systems. It is also working on upstream integration with AI frameworks, inference runtimes, and deployment environments. The stated goal is for standard models and tools to run on new hardware such as the D-series from the first day it is deployed.

Optical Connectivity and Quantum Development

Intel also pointed to its silicon photonics work, which uses light to move data over longer distances at what the company describes as a fraction of the energy of copper links. Intel did not attach figures or a product timeline to that claim.

On quantum, Intel restated the case for its proposed acquisition of Classiq , which would combine Classiq’s automated quantum algorithm synthesis platform with Intel’s silicon spin-qubit technology and chip manufacturing. Intel has said it expects the deal to close in the first half of 2027, pending regulatory approval.
